name: Project A: Environment / World Study
brief:
## Project Brief

Welcome to the first real studio-style project of the term! We will build three environment blockouts, and the three of them can each be different, different locations are fine. What has to hold is that each blockout has a clear purpose we can state in one sentence, and that the theme and feeling we are going for comes through at the final submission. The whole process follows the visual design pipeline: we block the space, we find the purpose and scale of each blockout, and we build the shapes so the audience always knows what matters. That is the Purpose, Scale, and Shape Hierarchy spine that runs through the whole class. The funpack-style presentation gives us a clean, scannable way to show our thinking alongside the work. Three clear blockouts beat one muddy render, and that is exactly how we measure success here.

The core deliverable is a **set of three environment blockouts, each with a clear purpose, presented in a funpack-style contact sheet**. The mood board and our weekly prep work round out the package. We will cover the weekly tools and steps in the lesson plan, so we can refer back to each week for the in-depth guidance. This brief is where the big picture lives.

## Themes and Timeframes

We have three different geographical themes to choose from, each rooted in a specific period, and within each theme there are three designs we can block out. We pick one theme, and the three designs we choose inside it become our three blockouts. The timeframe is not decoration. It tells us what props to place, what clothing to suggest, and what architecture to trust. Pick the theme we can see the clearest idea of, then the three designs we can commit to. Here is what is on the table:

**Theme 1: Nordic Fjords and Forests (10th to 12th Century)**. Timber and stone define the built world here, cold light defines the look, and low timber framing with sod roofs carries the architecture. Choose from the **Longhouse Hearth**: a timber longhouse interior built around a raised fire pit, with benches along the long walls and a carved rune stone on a rough stone shelf as the focal point; the **Coastal Fishing Hut**: a small single-room hut at the water's edge, with nets and rope from the rafters and dried cod by the door as the focal point; or the **Mountain Hermit Cell**: a cramped stone cell cut into the rock, with a thin bed, a birch shelf, and a worn psalter open on the shelf as the focal point. Props from the era: iron-tanged axes, wool cloaks, wooden bowls, whalebone combs.

**Theme 2: East Asian Mountain Temples (8th to 10th Century)**. Lacquered wood and paper define the interiors, and timber framing with tiled roofs carries the architecture. Choose from the **Kyoto Tea House Interior**: a low wooden room with tatami flooring, with shoji screens on one wall, a low table at center, and a single ceramic vessel on that table as the focal point; the **Rice Terrace Rest House**: an open-sided shelter at the edge of the rice terraces, with a crate and a bench, the terracing visible through the open side, and a weathered wooden bowl on the crate as the focal point; or the **Floating Market Stall**: a covered stall set on a waterway, with woven baskets and hanging goods, and a carved jade pendant resting on a cloth as the focal point. Props from the era: bronze mirrors, incense burners, silk sutra scrolls, lacquerware.

**Theme 3: Sahel Crossroads (13th to 15th Century)**. Rammed earth and carved wood define the built world here, and mud-brick walls with wooden toron beams and carved doorways carry the architecture. Choose from the **Granary Compound Interior**: a walled courtyard of rammed-earth rooms, with carved wooden doors, woven mats on the floor, and a leather water skin on the mats as the focal point; the **Cliffside Library**: a stone reading room set into a cliff face, with a low reading stone, a shelf of bound manuscripts, and a metal inkwell on the reading stone as the focal point; or the **Savanna Lookout**: a raised thatched platform with a low wall, with woven patterns on the walls, a wooden peg, and a curved bow on the peg as the focal point. Props from the era: cowrie shell strings, leather-bound manuscripts, clay water jugs, woven baskets.

Each blockout carries a *purpose*, and that purpose is a story beat, not just a postcard of a place. A beat has a before and an after: something just happened or is about to happen. A library is a noun, but the environment the moment a rare text lands on one of its tables is a beat. That difference is the heart of the whole project, and it is the thing we state in one sentence at Checkpoint A1. If a beat edges toward a heavier historical layer, we lead with the design question and the story hook first, and treat the historical context as optional background. The design carries the grade, not the history lesson.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Dream Worlds: Production Design for Animation* by Hans Bacher, Chapter 3, "Visual Development and Research."

## Project Details

The weekly lessons will walk us through the tools and techniques step by step, so we can refer back to each week for the detailed guidance on blocking, lighting, materials, camera work, and rendering. Here is the overview of what to expect:

We start with a **starter scene** that gives us an organized file with collections, a camera, and a three-point light rig ready to go. The **Quick Sheet renderer** helps us produce a contact sheet of our three blockouts in one pass. The **file auditor** checks naming and scene hygiene before we deliver. We will use **EEVEE for daily iteration** and reserve longer renders for the delivery pass. **Week 3** introduces skyboxes: we build custom skies and clouds to set the atmosphere. **Week 4** is about adding quick details, variations, and lighting impressions to bring the scene to life. Blender is the tool for the term, and the concepts stay version-agnostic.

Two in-class checkpoints will keep us on track, each gated on a working artifact rather than the clock. **Checkpoint A1** at week two reviews our three blockouts for scale and flow. **Checkpoint A2** at week three reviews our three blockouts for genuine variety. Delivery happens at week four with the three blockout renders, funpack presentation, mood board, and a clean file. At delivery we want to hear the process, not the polish. What we killed and why is more interesting than the finished image.

## Grading Rubric

The rubric for this project covers checkpoint criteria, final submission criteria, and how the grade is calculated across the three term projects. We self-assess before the instructor grades, and that comparison between our own read and the instructor's read is where the real learning happens. The full rubric breaks each dimension down with point values and rationale, so take a look before we start. The process and the thinking carry more weight than the final polish, and that is by design.

## Deliverables

- **Three environment blockouts**, each with a clear purpose we can state in one sentence.
- A **funpack-style presentation** assembled from the three blockout renders, with the theme and feeling of each one coming through.
- A **mood board** with research references.
- A clean **.blend**, auditor-checked.

Not required: animation, texture-baking, or a game-ready asset. This is design and presentation, and that is the whole of it.

## Checkpoints

Two in-class checkpoints, each gating on a **working artifact**, not the clock. Checkpoints are due **Wednesday after the assignment** (marked Thursday). Answer the self-checks before we show the work.

### A1: Blockout review (Wk 2)

- **What to show:** the three blockouts, with basic scale and flow established in each.
- **Focus criterion:** Does each blockout have **readable scale and a clear path through it**, or is it still a floating box with no sense of place?
- **Self-check before we show:**
  1. What is the purpose of each of the three blockouts, in one sentence?
  2. Does the scale read against the mannequin in each, and where does the eye go?
  3. If we walked through each space, what would we see first?

### A2: Blockout variety review (Wk 3)

- **What to show:** the contact sheet of the three blockouts showing genuine variety.
- **Focus criterion:** Do our three blockouts show **different choices**, or three copies of the same idea?
- **Self-check before we show:**
  1. Which blockout is the weakest, and what specifically makes it weak?
  2. What did we kill from early ideas, and why?
  3. Does each blockout carry its story beat, or is it just a pretty environment?

### Delivery A (Wk 4)

The three blockout renders, funpack presentation, mood board, and the clean .blend. At delivery we want to hear the process, not the polish. What we killed and why is more interesting than the finished image.

## Links and Resources

Here is where we will keep useful links and reference images as the term progresses. For now, the weekly lessons are the primary source of in-depth guidance, and the rubric is our grading compass. As we build, we will add mood board references, tool tips, and example funpacks right here.

*Coming soon: mood board templates, funpack examples, and reference image links.*
rubric:
*Three worlds, three timeframes. Fall 2026. Read this rubric like a conversation, not a form.*

## How This Term Is Graded

The term is split across three projects, weighted to keep the work steady from start to finish:

- **Project A = 30%** of the term grade
- **Project B = 30%** of the term grade
- **Project C = 40%** of the term grade

Project C carries the most weight because it is the heaviest build. The split makes sure we invest effort throughout the term, not just at the end.

Each project is scored on a 100-point scale. The final submission score becomes the project score, which is then weighted by the project percentage above. So a 75 out of 100 on Project A contributes 22.5 points (75 * 0.30) toward the term total.

## How Each Project Is Scored

Every project is split 50/50 between checkpoints and the final submission:

- **Checkpoints = 50% of the project score** (50 points available)
- **Final Submission = 50% of the project score** (50 points available)

This means checkpoints are not a formality. Half our project grade is locked in before the final delivery, and that is intentional. We want the climb to be visible, and we want the process to carry weight.

## Checkpoints

Checkpoints are due **Wednesday after the assignment**. We mark them **Thursday**. This timing is not flexible. The ability to deliver on time is incredibly important. In a real studio, a missed deadline is a missed deadline, and we want the practice to land now.

Each checkpoint has exactly **one criterion**: the focus of that week's lesson. We score it out of 25 points, so two checkpoints give us the 50 checkpoint points total.

### A1: Blockout Review (Wk 2) | 25 pts

**Criterion:** Does each blockout have readable scale and a clear path through it?

This is the only thing we are looking for at this stage. Not the materials, not the lighting, not the final camera. Just: can we walk through each space and feel like it is a place?

- **20 to 25 pts:** The space reads as a real location. A human dropped in would feel the right size. There is a path the eye can follow and a focal point the eye can land on.
- **15 to 19 pts:** The space is recognizable but scale wavers in places. The path is there but the eye gets lost partway through.
- **1 to 14 pts:** The space reads more like a floating object than a place we can inhabit. Scale is unclear and there is no obvious path.

### A2: Blockout Variety Review (Wk 3) | 25 pts

**Criterion:** Do our three blockouts show genuinely different choices?

Not three copies of the same render with the light nudged. Different compositions, different palettes, different focal points. Range, not repetition.

- **20 to 25 pts:** The blockouts are meaningfully different. We can point to specific choices that shift between blockouts and say why each one is worth exploring.
- **15 to 19 pts:** The blockouts have some variety, but two or more are too close to each other. The range is there but not sharp.
- **1 to 14 pts:** The blockouts feel like the same idea repeated. There is not enough difference between blockouts to call them a range.

## Final Submission Criteria

The final submission is scored out of 100 points. Those 100 points are then halved to give us the 50 points for the final submission portion of the project grade. Here are the four criteria:

### 1. Adherence to Reference Material | 30 pts

**Why it matters:** Directors look at this first. Can we take a brief, research it, and deliver work that matches the assigned style and world? This is the core job skill.

We are graded on how well our environment lives inside the chosen theme, its timeframe, and its design. Does the **10th-century Nordic Fjord** read as stone, timber, and cold light? Does the **9th-century East Asian Mountain Temple** carry lacquered wood, paper screens, and morning mist? Does the **14th-century Sahel Crossroads** feel like rammed earth, carved wood, and golden warmth? The timeframe shapes the props we place, the architecture we trust, and the clothing we suggest. The reference material is our north star, not a suggestion.

### 2. Presentation | 30 pts

**Why it matters:** Directors look at this second. Can we make our work legible to someone who has not seen the process? A great idea trapped behind a messy deliverable does not land.

This covers the funpack-style contact sheet, the mood board, the three blockouts, and how clearly the theme and feeling of each one comes through at the final submission. The presentation is communication, not decoration.

### 3. Design Innovation | 20 pts

**Why it matters:** This is the cool factor. Did we bring something to the table that makes us stand out, even within the reference constraints? Directors want work that surprises, and they want to hire people who do that.

We are looking for smart choices that go beyond the brief without violating it. A camera angle that tells the beat more clearly than a head-on shot. A palette that carries mood without drifting from the world. A detail that says "this was a real place" without reading as clutter.

### 4. Organization | 20 pts

**Why it matters:** Quality of life. Someone else needs to be able to open our file and follow along. Clean names, sorted collections, a readable node graph. This is not busywork. It is how we keep our own sanity.

The file auditor runs before delivery. If the auditor flags issues, those are fixable, and fixing them before we deliver is part of the grade.

## Summary

| Component | Points | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Checkpoint A1 | 25 pts | 25% of project grade |
| Checkpoint A2 | 25 pts | 25% of project grade |
| Final Submission (100 pts, halved) | 50 pts max | 50% of project grade |
| **Total Project A** | **100 pts** | **30% of term grade** |

The grade is not the render. The grade is the thinking we can defend, the decisions we can explain, and the evidence that we got there by working, not by luck. Everything else in this document is just the shape of that, aimed at our blockouts.

name: Project B — Character or Prop Design Package (Funpacks)
prompt:
**Pick one of three genre tracks, then pick your subject within it.** The subject is a starting point, not a mandate. We have full choice of what to design, even within a genre.

**Horror.** A creature, a cursed or haunted object, or a figure that reads as other. Design-level menace only, built from shape and silhouette and wrongness. Find the menace in the silhouette first.

**Comedy.** A gag prop, an exasperated sidekick, or an absurd machine or creature. It must read in silhouette and expression. If the joke only lands with a caption the design is not carrying it.

**Mythic or folklore.** A figure or artifact rooted in the world of Project A's theme so the subject belongs in the same place you built. If your Project A world is Nordic, design a guardian of the longhouse hearth, a mountain hermit, a coastal spirit of the fjords, or a carved rune figure given life. If East Asian, design a temple attendant, a spirit of the mountain mist, a guardian of the tea house, or a yokai of the rice terraces. If Sahel, design a scholar of the cliffside library, a guardian of the granary compound, or a spirit of the trade routes. Other strong anchors include a kitsune or yokai, a feathered serpent or jaguar deity, a koi or dragon, a Polynesian demigod.

The content note: keep horror and comedy at the design level. Shape, silhouette, menace, expression, absurdity. Where the subject carries historical or cultural weight, lead with the design question and the hook. Treat deeper context as optional background. The design carries the grade. Do the small amount of research that keeps the work from reading as a costume. A real simurgh is a griffin with a human head, not a generic dragon in a hat. That care is visible and it is part of the craft.
brief:
*One subject, presented the way a studio would hand it off.*

Welcome to the second project of the term. We built a place in Project A. Now we build the thing that lives in it. A character or a prop, developed in 3D, and presented as a **funpack**, the turnaround-and-studies sheet a production actually uses. A render shows one angle. A funpack says *this is the design, from every angle, and here is how it behaves.*

## What we are making

We design **one character or one prop** and present it as a production-ready reference sheet. A 3-view turnaround. A set of expressions or variants. A silhouette check. One or two material directions. Two hero renders. We are not making a game-ready model or a rig. We are making a design that reads and a sheet that communicates it. A funpack is not a portrait. It is a *specification*. When a production artist looks at our sheet they should be able to rebuild our subject in another shot from that sheet alone. If the back view is a mystery the design is not finished.

## The prompt

**Pick one of three genre tracks, then pick your subject within it.** The subject is a starting point, not a mandate. We have full choice of what to design, even within a genre.

**Horror.** A creature, a cursed or haunted object, or a figure that reads as other. Design-level menace only, built from shape and silhouette and wrongness. Find the menace in the silhouette first.

**Comedy.** A gag prop, an exasperated sidekick, or an absurd machine or creature. It must read in silhouette and expression. If the joke only lands with a caption the design is not carrying it.

**Mythic or folklore.** A figure or artifact rooted in the world of Project A's theme so the subject belongs in the same place you built. If your Project A world is Nordic, design a guardian of the longhouse hearth, a mountain hermit, a coastal spirit of the fjords, or a carved rune figure given life. If East Asian, design a temple attendant, a spirit of the mountain mist, a guardian of the tea house, or a yokai of the rice terraces. If Sahel, design a scholar of the cliffside library, a guardian of the granary compound, or a spirit of the trade routes. Other strong anchors include a kitsune or yokai, a feathered serpent or jaguar deity, a koi or dragon, a Polynesian demigod.

The content note: keep horror and comedy at the design level. Shape, silhouette, menace, expression, absurdity. Where the subject carries historical or cultural weight, lead with the design question and the hook. Treat deeper context as optional background. The design carries the grade. Do the small amount of research that keeps the work from reading as a costume. A real simurgh is a griffin with a human head, not a generic dragon in a hat. That care is visible and it is part of the craft.

## Guardrail menu

Every tool is available, never a hard dependency. If it is down the manual path works and the requirement does not change.

| Tool or technique | What it does for this project | Manual fallback |
|---|---|---|
| **Funpack or turnaround generator** | Places cameras around the subject and renders a labeled grid sheet | Set up 3 to 4 cameras manually, render each to PNG, assemble a labeled grid |
| **Quick Sheet renderer** | A contact sheet of variants or angles at low samples | Render each variant to its own PNG and assemble a grid by hand |
| **File or scene auditor** | Checks naming, orphan data, collection hygiene before delivery | Manually rename, purge orphans, confirm every collection has a purpose |
| **Palette extractor** (optional) | Swatches from a render for the material direction | Pick 3 to 5 values by eye |
| **Add-on allow-list** | Smart UV Project, BlenderKit, studio light kit, optionally Node Tools | Model the subject ourselves, use a sky texture or simple HDRI, light with a three-point rig |
| **Principled BSDF + EEVEE** | The material study, one or two believable or stylized directions | Build the material from the BSDF node by hand |
| **Render** | EEVEE for iteration, Cycles-class for the two hero renders | Bump EEVEE samples and GI for the heroes |

## Deliverables

- A **3-view funpack or turnaround** with front, side, back and often 3/4, with scale
- An **expression sheet** for character work or a **variant or palette sheet** for prop work, 3 to 5 reads
- A **silhouette check sheet** with flat-color renders at key angles, judged by one question: does it read in solid black
- **1 to 2 material directions**, believable or stylized
- **2 hero renders**, a day and a night pass
- A clean **.blend** file, auditor-checked

Not required: a full rig, animation, or a game-ready asset. Those belong to a later semester. This is design and presentation.

## Checkpoints

Two in-class checkpoints, each gating on a **working artifact**.

### B1: Proportions and blockout review (Wk 5)

Show the subject blocked out, plus at least one expression or variant started. The pass question: does the subject have a **readable silhouette and a clear proportion**.

### B2: Funpack and studies review (Wk 6)

Show the turnaround, the expression or variant sheet, and the silhouette check, with materials started. The pass question: does the sheet **communicate the design from every angle**.

### Delivery B (Wk 9, midterm crit)

The full funpack, the silhouette sheet, the two hero renders, and the clean .blend. Study Week (Wk 8) is our buffer between the last build week and delivery. At the crit the talk-through should be about process. What we tried, what we killed, and why the survivor won.

## Assessment focus

The four rubric dimensions land on the subject like this:

- **Adherence:** the genre intent comes through in design, not decoration. We can say why the silhouette reads the way it does.
- **Presentation:** the funpack is clear and consistent from every angle. The silhouette check is honest. The renders read at small size. The .blend is clean.
- **Innovation:** the expressions or variants are real choices. The materials explore at least two directions.
- **Organization:** we explored and then committed. The studies show weak variants killed and survivors built on. The process is visible.

The one line that does the most work: the genre has to be in the design, not stuck on top of it. A horror subject with a clean silhouette and a wrong proportion beats a horror subject with a great texture.

## Revisit (spacing hook)

Remember the three blockouts from Project A, where we checked that three reads were three choices, not three copies. Same test, different subject. Now it is expressions or variants. The question is identical: is each one a different decision or the same one nudged. It is about to show up in Project C, where a whole shot list has to pass this exact test.

---

**Three lines to close, specific to this project:**
- **What we did:** picked our genre and our subject, blocked it out, and started one variant.
- **What we learned:** a funpack is a specification, and the back view is part of the design, not an afterthought.
- **What we would try next:** flattening the silhouette to solid black and asking what we actually see before we add any color.
rubric:
*One subject, presented the way a studio would hand it off. Fall 2026. This is the rubric for Project B, applied to the funpack, the two checkpoints, and the delivery. Read it like a conversation, not a form.*

Project B counts for **30% of the term grade**. It is scored on a 100-point scale, then weighted by 0.30 to contribute toward the term total.

## How Project B is scored

The project splits 50/50 between checkpoints and the final submission.

- **Checkpoints = 50% of the project score** (50 points available). Two checkpoints, each scored on one criterion, 25 points each.
- **Final Submission = 50% of the project score** (50 points available). Four criteria: **Adherence** (30%), **Presentation** (30%), **Innovation** (20%), **Organization** (20%).

Checkpoints are due **Wednesday after the assignment**. We mark them **Thursday**. This timing is not flexible.

## What we are delivering (checklist)

- **A 3-view funpack or turnaround** with front, side, back, and often 3/4, with scale. The subject built all the way around, not just a nice front.
- **An expression sheet** for character work or a **variant or palette sheet** for prop work, three to five reads. Real choices, not the same face with a different mouth.
- **A silhouette check sheet** with flat-color renders at key angles, judged by one question: does it read in solid black.
- **One to two material directions**, believable or stylized. The *what it is made of and why*, not glossy brown.
- **Two hero renders**, a day and a night pass, so the design is tested in two lights.
- **A clean .blend file**, auditor-checked. Named, organized, no orphan data.
- **A talk-through at delivery.** The process, not the polish. What we tried, what we killed, and why the survivor won.

## Checkpoint gates

Both gate on a **working artifact, not on time**. Hit the pass question, move on. Miss it and we fix it in class, and that fix is part of our iteration evidence, not a penalty.

### B1: Proportions and blockout review (Wk 5) | 25 pts

**Criterion:** Does the subject have a readable silhouette and a clear proportion.

Show the subject blocked out, plus at least one expression or variant started.

- **Strong:** the silhouette reads in solid black. The proportion lands the genre. A horror figure with a wrong ratio that creates unease. A comedy prop where the shape itself is the joke. The center of gravity is clear and the subject looks stable.
- **Not there yet:** a blob wearing a costume. The silhouette is generic. The proportions do not serve the genre. The subject could belong to any track.

### B2: Funpack and studies review (Wk 6) | 25 pts

**Criterion:** Does the sheet communicate the design from every angle.

Show the turnaround, the expression or variant sheet, and the silhouette check, with materials started.

- **Strong:** the back view is as intentional as the front. The variants show real decisions. The silhouette check changed something about the design. The material direction serves the genre.
- **Not there yet:** the front is beautiful and the back is a surprise. The variants are the same idea nudged. The silhouette was rendered but never used as a filter.

## Final submission criteria (50 points total)

### Adherence (30%)

Does the genre intent land in the design, not stuck on top of it. Can we say why the silhouette reads the way it does.

- **Strong:** the one-sentence *what it is about* is real. The volume, the face, the material, and the light all serve it. A horror subject with a clean silhouette and a wrong proportion. A comedy prop that reads the joke in silhouette. When asked *why this one and not the other* the answer is a reason, not a feeling. The genre is in the design.
- **Not there yet:** a beautiful subject that needs a caption to land. A texture doing the design job. The back is a mystery. The genre is there but we cannot say where it is.

### Presentation (30%)

Does the sheet communicate the design from every angle. Is the craft of showing the work clean and professional.

- **Strong:** the turnaround is built from clean, readable volumes. The silhouette check shows the subject reads in solid black, from front, side, and back. The day and night heroes prove the subject is portable and survives a light it did not choose. The file is named and organized. The weak variants are shown as *killed*, not hidden.
- **Not there yet:** the front is beautiful and the back is a surprise. The silhouette needs details to be recognized, which means the face is doing the silhouette job. The night hero is just a dark version of the day one.

### Innovation (20%)

Are the expressions or variants real choices. Do the materials explore at least two directions.

- **Strong:** the variants are kinds of the same thing, each one a real alternative we could have shipped. A curious djinn has a curious tilt, a curious squint, a curious lean, and we can pick the one that serves the beat. The materials explore the used and the new, or the smooth and the rough, and each one serves the design sentence.
- **Not there yet:** five faces that are the same face with a different mouth. One material with the roughness nudged. The work looks nice and says one thing. We made a portrait, not a set of options.

### Organization (20%)

Can we see the climb. Did we explore and then commit. Is the process visible.

- **Strong:** we killed the nudge and kept the real alternative. The silhouette check is there and it changed something. The material list shows we knew what to fix and why before we rendered the pair. The day or night test told us where the subject quietly falls apart. The .blend is named, organized, and free of orphan data.
- **Not there yet:** only the survivor. The heroes are there and the process is not. We cannot see how the decisions were made, and we cannot tell a good decision from a lucky one. The file is messy or unorganized.

## Self-assess before we hand it in

These are the Boud moves. We answer them in our three-line reflection, honestly, before we hand the work over. The instructor reads them and tells us where their view matches ours and where it does not.

- What changed between our B1 blockout and our delivery, and why. If the answer is *we made it prettier* that is execution. If it is *we killed the variant that was a nudge and the silhouette got cleaner* that is design.
- What is the one-sentence *what it is about* for our subject, and does the silhouette actually show it. If the sentence says *curious, not scary* and the silhouette says *a spiky lump* the subject is working against the sentence.
- Which of our variants or material directions is the weakest, and what specifically is weak about it. Naming our own weak work, precisely, is the whole of decision quality.
- Does our subject lead without trapping. Put it in a scene we did not design, in a hard shadow, in a cool light. Does it still lead.

---

**One line to carry out of this rubric:** the grade is not the render. The grade is the thinking we can defend, the decisions we can explain, and the evidence that we got there by working, not by luck. On B the one line that does the most work: the genre is in the design, not stuck on top of it.

name: Project C — Scene / Previs Blockout (Capstone)
prompt:
**The beat comes from Project A's beat bank.** It inherits our world and our tone. Pick the **P1 shortlist beat** we already chose, with its fantastical hook. If we are in the Nordic theme, that might be a spirit emerging from the fjord mist. If East Asian, a lantern ceremony at dawn in the mountain temple. If Sahel, a caravan arriving at the cliffside library as the last light fades. We know ours.

**The continuity requirement.** Across all our shots, the camera stays on **one side of the action axis**, the invisible line between the two main elements of the scene. Cross that line and the geography flips. Staying on one side is the difference between a shot list and a confusion.

> **Content note:** the beat inherits Project A's policy. **Lead with the design question and the hook** — the space, the light, the moment — and treat any heavier historical or cultural layer as optional background. The design and the story carry the grade, not the sensitive context. Keep horror and comedy at the design level, as in Project B.

**Motivated cameras are the whole grade of this project.** Every camera we place has a reason it is at that height, that distance, that angle, tied to the beat. The character is looking left, so the camera is where we see them look. The reveal is the point, so the wide shot comes before the close one. The pretty frame that is parked for no reason is the one we cut.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 4, "Composing for Continuity."** "The line," the point of reference, and why crossing it reads as a jump — that chapter is the entire continuity half of this project, spelled out with case studies. Read it before C1.
brief:
*One small story, told with cameras that have a reason to be where they are.*

## The brief

Project A gave us a place. Project B gave us a subject. This is where they meet and something small actually *happens*.

We block a short scene. We place our subject in our world. We move a camera through it with a reason. This is previs, the cheap storyboard, and it is the closest we get in this track to how a real production validates a scene before anyone touches final work. No Grease Pencil. No animation. Just still frames, in order, that tell a beat. That is the capstone.

## What we are making

We take the **story beat from Project A** and place our **B subject** inside it. We block the scene at rough scale. We set **motivated cameras** — an establishing shot plus two or three beats. We keep **180-degree continuity** across every shot. We present it as a **shot-sequence contact sheet** with static frames, labeled, in story order.

We are not making a film. We are making the *proof* that the scene works before it becomes one.

## The prompt

**The beat comes from Project A's beat bank.** It inherits our world and our tone. Pick the **P1 shortlist beat** we already chose, with its fantastical hook. If we are in the Nordic theme, that might be a spirit emerging from the fjord mist. If East Asian, a lantern ceremony at dawn in the mountain temple. If Sahel, a caravan arriving at the cliffside library as the last light fades. We know ours.

**The continuity requirement.** Across all our shots, the camera stays on **one side of the action axis**, the invisible line between the two main elements of the scene. Cross that line and the geography flips. Staying on one side is the difference between a shot list and a confusion.

> **Content note:** the beat inherits Project A's policy. **Lead with the design question and the hook** — the space, the light, the moment — and treat any heavier historical or cultural layer as optional background. The design and the story carry the grade, not the sensitive context. Keep horror and comedy at the design level, as in Project B.

**Motivated cameras are the whole grade of this project.** Every camera we place has a reason it is at that height, that distance, that angle, tied to the beat. The character is looking left, so the camera is where we see them look. The reveal is the point, so the wide shot comes before the close one. The pretty frame that is parked for no reason is the one we cut.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 4, "Composing for Continuity."** "The line," the point of reference, and why crossing it reads as a jump — that chapter is the entire continuity half of this project, spelled out with case studies. Read it before C1.

## Guardrail menu

Every tool is **available**, never a hard dependency. Manual fallbacks keep the requirement intact if one is down.

| Tool / technique | What it does for this project | Manual fallback |
|---|---|---|
| **Quick Sheet renderer** | Builds the **shot-sequence contact sheet** in one render | Render each camera to PNG, number them, lay them into a labeled grid in a 2D app |
| **Variant / sequence composer** | Sequence mode for arranging the shot sheet | Assemble the frames by hand in a 2D app |
| **File / scene auditor** | Checks naming, orphan data, collection hygiene | Manually rename, purge orphans, confirm every collection has a purpose |
| **Add-on allow-list** | Smart UV Project, BlenderKit, a studio light kit, optionally Node Tools | Reuse the props and materials from A and B; light with a three-point rig from lamps |
| **Paintover** | Design accents over the blockout, in a 2D app | Any 2D app: **Photoshop, Procreate, Clip Studio** — the skill is the paintover, not the app |
| **Render** | **EEVEE** for iteration; Cycles-class for hero passes | Bump EEVEE samples and GI, or run a longer Cycles-class pass |

Blender is **5.x** all term. This project mostly *re-uses* what A and B taught us, plus two new ideas: motivated cameras and 180-degree continuity.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Dream Worlds: Production Design for Animation* by Hans Bacher, **Chapter 6, "Camera Rules."** The shot sizes, the 180-degree invisible line, the floor plans for movement and continuity. Pair it with the *Framed Ink* continuity chapter above.

## Deliverables

- A **previs blockout** of the scene, with our A environment and our B subject placed, at rough scale.
- **Motivated cameras**, an establishing shot plus 2 to 3 beats, each chosen for the beat.
- **180-degree continuity** maintained across all shots, the camera stays on one side of the action axis.
- **Paintover accents** that add design intent over the blockout.
- A **light / mood turn across the sequence**, with lighting and mood changing deliberately from beat to beat to carry the emotional turn. We **name the turn**: what changes, how it changes, and why it is the right turn.
- A **shot-sequence contact sheet**, a sequence of still frames in story order, each labeled with type and purpose.
- A clean **.blend**, auditor-checked.

Motion, full animation, and 4K are not required. This is a sequence of stills that tells a beat. The label on each frame matters as much as the frame — *establishing, beat, reveal* — because that is how a production reads it.

## Checkpoints

Two in-class checkpoints, each gating on a **working artifact**, not the clock.

### C1 — Shot list / story-beats review (Wk 10)

- **What to show:** our shot list, with the beats in order, the type and purpose of each, where each camera sits relative to the action axis, and the **emotional turn of the beat** (the mood at the start and where it goes).
- **Pass question:** does the list **tell the beat in order**, with each shot motivated.
- **Self-check:**
  1. Read the shots in order. Where does the story *move*, and which shot is doing the moving?
  2. Draw the action axis on a napkin. Which side is every camera on?
  3. Which single shot, cut, would we lose nothing by removing? Cut it.
  4. What is the emotional turn of the beat? Name it. That turn is the target our light plan will hit by C2.

### C2 — Blockout + camera review (Wk 12)

- **What to show:** the blocked scene with cameras placed, the 180-degree line holding, and the light / mood turn set.
- **Pass question:** is the camera **motivated and continuous**.
- **Self-check:**
  1. For each camera, name its motivation — what in the scene justifies it being exactly there.
  2. Where is the line, and did we stay on one side?
  3. If the frames play in order, does the scene read as one continuous moment?
  4. Can we **name the light / mood turn**, and does the contact sheet show it legibly?

### Delivery C (Wk 14, final crit)

The full contact sheet, the paintover accents, the clean .blend, and the talk-through. **Wk 13 is the grace week** — catch-up, polish, or absorbing an emergency. No hard gate. Nothing lands on a cliff.

At the final crit, the talk-through covers the story we told: what the beat was, why each camera, and what we cut. That talk-through *is* a graded deliverable, and it is where the design thinking shows.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Setting the Scene: The Art & Evolution of Animation Layout* by Fraser MacLean, **Chapter 7, "The Story Reel and Beyond."** The story reel to the virtual camera is the exact lineage of what previs is. Good context for why this project exists.

## Assessment focus

For this project the four rubric dimensions land like this:

- **Design range:** the shots are a *sequence* of different framings and purposes, not the same wide shot three times.
- **Decision quality:** every camera is motivated, the 180-degree line is respected, and the genre and tone from A and B reads clearly through the choices.
- **Execution + presentation:** the contact sheet is labeled and in story order, the light / mood turn reads legibly across the frames, the paintover adds intent, and the .blend is clean.
- **Iteration evidence:** C1 to C2 to delivery is a visible climb. The shot list got cut and re-ordered. The weak cameras got removed. The process is legible in what survived.

The bar is one line: **a stranger watching our frames in order should understand the beat, the tone, and why the camera is where it is.** If they do, we have done it.

## Revisit (spacing hook)

Remember that scale problem from Project A, where we had to decide whether the library reads as *grand* or as *a hallway*. It is back, wearing a different hat. Now it is not the space deciding — it is the **camera**. A wide lens from close in makes a small room feel vast. A long lens from far away makes a courtyard feel cramped. Same muscle, new tool.

And remember the directional-study test from A and B — is each shot a different *choice*. That test is now our whole shot list. We have been practicing it for a month. Use it.

*This is the last project. After the final crit, Semester 4 is where the polish and the portfolio happen. For now, we just have to prove the ideas work. They do. Show me.*

---

**Three lines to close, specific to this week:**
- **What we did:** we took our A beat and B subject, blocked the scene, and placed a motivated camera on the right side of the line.
- **What we learned:** a camera with a reason beats a camera that is just pretty, and the line is the geography the audience trusts.
- **What we would try next:** cutting the weakest shot and seeing if the beat still lands, because it probably will.

*If the frame will not do what we want, that is a lens or a position question, not a you thing. Move the camera, re-render, compare. Ask.*
rubric:
*One small story, told with cameras that have a reason to be where they are. Fall 2026. This is the rubric for Project C, the capstone. Read it like a conversation, not a form.*

## How this term is graded

The term is split across three projects, weighted to keep the work steady from start to finish:

- **Project A = 30%** of the term grade
- **Project B = 30%** of the term grade
- **Project C = 40%** of the term grade

Project C carries the most weight because it is the heaviest build. The split makes sure we invest effort throughout the term, not just at the end.

Each project is scored on a 100-point scale. The final submission score becomes the project score, which is then weighted by the project percentage above. A 75 out of 100 on Project C contributes 30 points (75 * 0.40) toward the term total.

## How Project C is scored

Every project splits 50/50 between checkpoints and the final submission:

- **Checkpoints = 50% of the project score** (50 points available)
- **Final Submission = 50% of the project score** (50 points available)

This means checkpoints are not a formality. Half our project grade is locked in before the final delivery, and that is intentional. We want the climb to be visible, and we want the process to carry weight.

## What we are delivering (checklist)

Hold ourselves to this list before the final crit. If a line is missing, that is a finding, and it is the best possible time to find it.

- A **previs blockout of the scene**, with our A environment and our B subject placed, at rough scale. A place and a thing, doing a small thing together.
- **Motivated cameras**, an establishing shot plus two or three beats, each chosen for the beat, not by default. The character is looking left, so the camera is where we see them look.
- **180-degree continuity** across all shots, the camera stays on one side of the action axis. The geography the audience trusts.
- **Paintover accents**, re-used from Project A, that add design intent over the blockout.
- A **deliberate light / mood turn across the sequence**, with lighting and mood changing from beat to beat to carry the story's emotional turn, and we can name what changes, how, and why.
- A **shot-sequence contact sheet**, static by design, still frames in story order, each labeled with type and purpose. The one that demonstrates the light / mood turn, in order.
- A clean **.blend**, auditor-checked. Named, organized, no orphan data.
- A **talk-through at the final crit**, covering what the beat was, why each camera, what we cut, and the light / mood turn. This talk-through *is* a graded deliverable.

## Checkpoints

Checkpoints are due **Wednesday after the assignment**. We mark them **Thursday**. This timing is not flexible.

Each checkpoint has exactly **one criterion**: the focus of that week's lesson. We score it out of 25 points, so two checkpoints give us the 50 checkpoint points total.

### C1: Shot list / story-beats review (Wk 10) | 25 pts

**Criterion:** Does the shot list **tell the beat in order**, with each shot motivated?

This is the only thing we are looking for at this stage. Not the render quality, not the materials, not the lighting. Just: does the sequence read as a story, with each camera earning its place?

- **20 to 25 pts:** The shots are in story order, each with a clear type and purpose. The action axis is drawn and respected. The emotional turn of the beat is named. The sequence moves.
- **15 to 19 pts:** The list has the right shots but the order does not yet read as a story. One or two cameras lack a stated motivation. The emotional turn is not yet named.
- **1 to 14 pts:** The list reads as a pile of nice framings with no sequence. The action axis is missing or crossed. There is no emotional turn identified.

### C2: Blockout + camera review (Wk 12) | 25 pts

**Criterion:** Is the camera **motivated and continuous**, or is it parked in pretty spots?

At this stage the scene is blocked and the cameras are placed. The question is whether the geography holds and the cameras have reasons for being where they are.

- **20 to 25 pts:** Every camera has a named motivation. The 180-degree line holds across all shots. The light / mood turn is set and legible on the contact sheet. The scene reads as one continuous moment.
- **15 to 19 pts:** Most cameras are motivated but one or two feel parked. The line mostly holds but there is a wobble. The light / mood turn is started but not yet fully legible.
- **1 to 14 pts:** The cameras lack motivation. The line is crossed and the geography flips. The light / mood turn is not set or not visible. The frames read as disconnected moments.

## Final Submission Criteria

The final submission is scored out of 100 points. Those 100 points are then halved to give us the 50 points for the final submission portion of the project grade. Here are the four criteria:

### 1. Adherence to Reference Material | 30 pts

**Why it matters:** Directors look at this first. Can we take a brief, research it, and deliver work that matches the assigned style and world? This is the core job skill.

We are graded on how well our scene lives inside the world we built in Project A, with the subject we designed in Project B. Does the beat carry through from the environment to the previs? Does the genre and tone read consistently? Is the beat from Project A's beat bank legible in the final sequence? The reference world is our north star, not a suggestion.

### 2. Presentation | 30 pts

**Why it matters:** Directors look at this second. Can we make our work legible to someone who has not seen the process? A great idea trapped behind a messy deliverable does not land.

This covers the shot-sequence contact sheet, the labels on each frame, the light / mood turn reading clearly across the sequence, the paintover accents, the talk-through, and how cleanly the .blend is organized. The presentation is communication, not decoration. A stranger watching our frames in order should understand the beat, the tone, and why the camera is where it is.

### 3. Design Innovation | 20 pts

**Why it matters:** This is the cool factor. Did we bring something to the table that makes us stand out, even within the reference constraints? Directors want work that surprises, and they want to hire people who do that.

We are looking for smart choices that go beyond the brief without violating it. A camera angle that tells the beat more clearly than a head-on shot. A light / mood turn that carries emotional weight. A shot sequence that re-orders the expected beats into something that reads better. A detail in the paintover that says "this was a real place" without reading as clutter.

### 4. Organization | 20 pts

**Why it matters:** Quality of life. Someone else needs to be able to open our file and follow along. Clean names, sorted collections, a readable node graph. This is not busywork. It is how we keep our own sanity.

The file auditor runs before delivery. If the auditor flags issues, those are fixable, and fixing them before we deliver is part of the grade. Cut shots shown as *killed*, not hidden, count toward this dimension.

## Summary

| Component | Points | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Checkpoint C1 | 25 pts | 25% of project grade |
| Checkpoint C2 | 25 pts | 25% of project grade |
| Final Submission (100 pts, halved) | 50 pts max | 50% of project grade |
| **Total Project C** | **100 pts** | **40% of term grade** |

The grade is not the render. The grade is the thinking we can defend, the decisions we can explain, and the evidence that we got there by working, not by luck. Everything else in this document is just the shape of that, aimed at our scene.

## Self-assess before we hand it over

Answer these in our three-line reflection, honestly, before we hand the work over. The instructor reads them and tells us where the view matches and where it does not. That comparison is worth more than either one alone.

- **What changed between our C1 shot list and our delivery, and why?** If the answer is "we made it prettier," that is execution. If it is "we cut the weak shot and re-ordered the rest and the beat moved," that is design.
- **For each camera, what is the motivation, and does the 180-degree line hold across all of them?** If a camera is parked in a pretty spot for no reason, name it.
- **Which of our shots is the weakest, and what specifically is weak about it?** Naming our own weak work, precisely, is the whole of decision quality.
- **What is the light / mood turn, and can we defend it?** Name what changes from beat to beat, how it changes, why it is the right turn, and what we held so the scene still reads as one.
- **What would we change with another week?** A student who says "we are done" has stopped looking. A student who names one specific next move is still thinking.

---

**One line to carry out of this rubric:** the grade is not the render. The grade is the thinking we can defend, the decisions we can explain, and the evidence that we got there by working, not by luck. And on C, the one line that does the most work: **motivated is the whole grade of this project.** A stranger watching our frames in order should understand the beat, the tone, and why the camera is where it is.
